# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, affecting an estimated 64 million people globally [1]. Despite advances in guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) and device-based interventions such as cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), a substantial proportion of patients remain symptomatic [2]. Importantly, only approximately one-third of patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) have a wide QRS complex and are eligible for CRT [3]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) therapy has emerged as a device-based option for symptomatic HFrEF patients with narrow QRS who are not candidates for CRT [4].

## Mechanism of Action

CCM delivers non-excitatory electrical signals to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period of the cardiac action potential [5]. Because these signals are delivered when the myocardium cannot be depolarized, they do not initiate a new contraction but instead enhance the strength of the existing contraction [6]. The proposed mechanism involves modulation of intracellular calcium handling, with enhanced sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium uptake and increased phosphorylation of phospholamban [7]. Experimental studies have demonstrated reversal of the fetal gene program and normalization of key calcium-cycling proteins, including SERCA2a and the ryanodine receptor [8,9]. These molecular changes suggest that CCM may produce favorable reverse remodeling rather than merely acute inotropic effects [10].

## Clinical Evidence

The clinical development of CCM has been supported by several randomized controlled trials. The FIX-HF-4 study, a double-blind crossover trial, demonstrated improvements in peak oxygen consumption (peak VO2) and quality of life during active CCM treatment [11]. The FIX-HF-5 trial enrolled patients with NYHA class III–IV symptoms and ejection fraction ≤35%; while the primary endpoint of ventilatory anaerobic threshold was not met in the overall cohort, prespecified subgroup analyses suggested benefit in patients with ejection fraction between 25% and 45% [12]. This finding informed the design of the subsequent FIX-HF-5C trial, which confirmed significant improvements in peak VO2, six-minute walk distance, and quality of life in patients with ejection fraction between 25% and 45% [13].

A patient-level meta-analysis of randomized CCM trials reported consistent improvements in exercise tolerance and quality of life, along with a reduction in HF hospitalizations [14]. The FIX-HF-5C2 study extended these observations using a single-lead configuration, demonstrating comparable improvements in peak VO2 [15]. Real-world registries, including the CCM-REG study, have corroborated trial findings, showing sustained symptomatic improvement and reductions in HF hospitalization rates over follow-up [16,17].

Several studies have specifically evaluated quality of life and functional outcomes, demonstrating improvements in the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire score and NYHA functional class [18,19]. The durability of these benefits over long-term follow-up has been documented in multiple cohorts [20].

## Safety Considerations

CCM has demonstrated an acceptable safety profile across trials and registries [21]. The Optimizer system has not been associated with proarrhythmia, and CCM signals do not interfere with implantable cardioverter-defibrillator function when devices are appropriately programmed [22,23]. Procedural complications are comparable to those of other transvenous device implantations, including lead dislodgement and pocket-related events [24].

## Expanding Indications

While the primary evidence base concerns HFrEF, interest has grown in extending CCM to other populations. Preliminary data suggest potential benefit in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), and dedicated trials are ongoing [25,26]. CCM has also been studied in patients with atrial fibrillation, who were excluded from some pivotal trials, with encouraging results regarding feasibility and efficacy [27]. Additional investigations are exploring the role of CCM in patients with concomitant CRT devices and in those with more advanced disease [28].

## Guidelines and Future Directions

CCM received regulatory approval and has been incorporated into HF management algorithms for selected symptomatic HFrEF patients with narrow QRS despite optimal GDMT [29]. Current guidance positions CCM as an option for patients with NYHA class III symptoms, ejection fraction 25–45%, and QRS duration below 130 ms [29]. Future research priorities include adequately powered trials evaluating hard endpoints such as mortality, refinement of patient selection through biomarkers and imaging, and clarification of the role of CCM in HFpEF and atrial fibrillation populations [30].

## Conclusion

CCM therapy represents a valuable addition to the device armamentarium for symptomatic HFrEF patients ineligible for CRT. Robust evidence supports improvements in exercise capacity, quality of life, and HF hospitalizations, with a reassuring safety profile. Ongoing trials will define its role in broader HF phenotypes and establish its impact on long-term clinical outcomes.
